To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) for a class of realistic agendas, there exist aggregation procedures which are consistent and complete, and (ii) these procedures can be characterised by a simple condition on their acceptance thresholds.

the agenda of subjunctive implications is the largest class of agendas for which consistent collective judgment aggregation is possible, and that the class of quota rules that achieve this possibility is characterised by a simple condition on the thresholds.

the possibility of judgment aggregation depends on the way we model the propositions and that the possibility can be established for a wide class of agendas once we do not use the material implication to model the subjunctive implications.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the possibility of aggregation in realistic scenarios, where propositions are logically connected.
the possibility of judgment aggregation in a logic with subjunctive implication and with the general characterisation of aggregation in a general logic.
the question: what is the most general form of judgment aggregation?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there exists a wide class of agendas for which the impossibility results can be circumvented by modelling propositions as subjunctive rather than material implications.
the impossibility results are not a reason to despair, but a reason to look more closely at the agenda and the aggregation rule.
for agendas that are not too complicated, there are simple aggregation procedures that work well, and that there is no reason for pessimism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the impossibility results are only a problem for agendas with material implications.
, if we are interested in voting over logically connected propositions, we should not be too worried about the possibility of judgment aggregation.
the impossibility results for judgment aggregation do not apply if we use subjunctive implications and appropriate quota rules.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not necessary to give up independence of judgment aggregation in the case of logically connected propositions, as long as the logic of propositions is adequately modelled.
it is possible to reach collective judgments on logically connected propositions in many realistic cases.
the agenda structure matters, and that the agenda structure can be used to overcome the impossibility results.
